content: Breastfeeding should only cease when a nutritionally adequate and safe diet, excluding breast milk, can be provided to the infant. This recommendation updates the 2010 guidance on breastfeeding practices and the duration of breastfeeding. However, the core components of the 2010 recommendations regarding breastfeeding practices and cessation remain unchanged and valid. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines recommended breastfeeding practices as follows: (1) initiating breastfeeding within the first hour of life; (2) exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, meaning the infant receives only breast milk without any additional food or drink, not even water; (3) continued breastfeeding for up to two years of age or beyond, with the introduction of appropriate complementary foods at six months; and (4) breastfeeding on demand, as often as the child desires, both day and night. For mothers living with HIV who do not exclusively breastfeed, it is reassuring to note that antiretroviral therapy (ART) significantly reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in the context of mixed feeding. While exclusive breastfeeding is recommended, mixed feeding is not a reason to stop breastfeeding if ART is being administered. For mothers living with HIV who do not plan to breastfeed for 12 months, shorter durations of breastfeeding are still better than not initiating breastfeeding at all. Breastfeeding is a cornerstone of child survival, nutrition, development, and maternal health. It is particularly critical in settings where diarrhea, pneumonia, and undernutrition are leading causes of mortality among children under five years of age. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, followed by continued breastfeeding with appropriate complementary foods for up to two years or beyond. Evidence highlights the long-term benefits of extended breastfeeding for both maternal and child health, including child development and the prevention of noncommunicable diseases, underscoring the importance of supporting breastfeeding in all income settings. HIV infection directly impacts the nutritional status of women and children living with HIV and indirectly affects them by altering household food security and influencing inappropriate infant-feeding practices. In 2016, WHO updated its guidance on HIV and infant feeding based on revisions to antiretroviral drug guidelines, expanded evidence, and programmatic experience. These updates emphasize the importance of supporting mothers living with HIV in their chosen feeding practices, even when these differ from nationally recommended practices. Implementation of these recommendations requires training and capacity-building for healthcare workers to equip them with the necessary skills and tools, along with adequate supervision and oversight. Programs must be systematically monitored to ensure success and address challenges in implementation. Data collection on breastfeeding duration, ART adherence, and retention rates in care for mothers and infants is essential to improve service quality at local and district levels. Palliative care is a critical component of comprehensive clinical management for people living with HIV. It aims to prevent and relieve suffering while optimizing quality of life. Common issues managed by palliative care include pain, physical symptoms related to HIV or its treatment, mood disorders, psychosocial distress from stigma and poverty, and spiritual distress. The growing population of aging individuals living with HIV, many with multimorbidity, highlights the changing needs for palliative care. More than 90% of the palliative care needs among people living with HIV are in lowand middle-income countries, with children representing a significant proportion of this need. Unrelieved suffering among people living with HIV is substantial, with high prevalence rates of anxiety, depression, and physical symptoms such as fatigue, pain, nausea, and breathlessness. These burdens negatively impact quality of life, adherence to ART, and overall health outcomes. Palliative care seeks to address these challenges through early identification, accurate assessment, and treatment of physical, mental, social, and spiritual suffering. It enhances quality of life, promotes dignity, and provides support throughout the course of illness, including end-of-life care. Palliative care should be integrated with HIV prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services and made accessible at all levels of healthcare systems, including in individuals' homes. It is applicable from the point of diagnosis, enabling a holistic, person-centered approach that prioritizes individual preferences and symptom control. For people living with HIV at the end of life, palliative care addresses worsening symptoms, changing priorities, and decisions about treatment withdrawal and place of death. Palliative care is recognized as a human right and an essential component of integrated, people-centered health services. It should be actively supported by national health authorities, healthcare providers, and community members to ensure its availability and accessibility for all individuals in need.
